# Final presentation: speaker notes (generated by tools/build_deck.py; do not edit by hand)

Rui: slides 1–5 and 11–12. Khadijah: slides 6–10. About one minute per main slide.

## 1. Trace and Gate

Hi, I'm Rui, this is Khadijah. Our project is Trace and Gate: stopping prompt injection in email agents. (pause) Since the interim we froze our defenses, tested them on attacks they had never seen, on a second model and on AgentDojo, and measured a cost our first benchmark missed.

Key line: Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.

## 2. Every email is attacker input

An email assistant reads mail from anyone, and it can send, forward and delete for you. (pause) Alex asks it to open the sponsor's attachment. Hidden in the attachment is an instruction to forward the club's bank-PIN email to an outside address, and the undefended agent does it. (pause) OWASP ranks prompt injection the number one LLM risk, Microsoft collected over 200,000 attack prompts in a public challenge, and on our development benchmark 45% of attacks worked with no defense.

Key line: Every inbound email is attacker input.

## 3. Research question

Our question: do provenance tracking and policy checks stop hijacked email actions, compared with no defense and Dual-LLM, without breaking normal tasks? (pause) The thresholds are the ones from our proposal: at least 80% fewer successful attacks, and at most a 10-point drop in normal-task success. We test them on held-out attacks, pooled over three runs.

Key line: Safe, and still useful, on attacks we never tuned for.

## 4. Where each defense acts

This is where each defense sits between an email and an action. (pause) Dual-LLM changes what the model reads: a second model turns each email into variables. D2 and D1h check what the model does. D2 asks: is this tool, recipient and email on the task's allowlist? D1h asks: does every argument, the recipient, the link, the target, trace back to the user? (pause) If either says no, the call is blocked with a neutral error, and the agent can still finish the user's task.

Key line: B1 changes what the model reads; D1h and D2 check what it does.

## 5. Benchmark and test setup

We test on four sets. The development suite of 153 tasks is where we built and debugged. Then we froze the defenses on 24 October, and only after that built a held-out set: the same normal tasks, 40 new LLMail-Inject attacks and 18 attacks we wrote ourselves in styles the defenses had never seen. (pause) Two more sets check the edges: 40 normal tasks that contain harmless links, and AgentDojo's workspace suite. Everything ran on Qwen3-8B at temperature 0.3, scored by code from the final mailbox. Over to Khadijah.

Key line: Frozen first, then tested on attacks the defenses never saw.

## 6. Development: attacks 45% → 0%, no normal task lost

First, development. With no defense, 45.4% of attacks worked. With any of the four defenses, none did. (pause) The zeros are earned: under D1h+D2 the model still tried the attacker's action 8 times, and every attempt was blocked. And D1h+D2 completed 89.3% of normal tasks, the same as no defense.

Key line: Every defense reached zero, and D1h+D2 lost no normal task.

## 7. Held-out: attacks 22% → 0%, three runs

Now the real test: attacks written after the freeze. Pooled over three runs, 21.8% of held-out attacks worked with no defense, and 0.0% under every defense; under D1h+D2 the model still tried the attacker's action 19 times, all blocked. (pause) One honest caveat: the 18 attacks we wrote ourselves never worked, not even with no defense: 0/54. So they don't test the defenses; all 38 successes came from the 40 new LLMail-Inject emails, 31.7% of them with no defense. (pause) Normal tasks: D1h+D2 91.7% against 89.3% with no defense, +2.4 points. Paired test against no defense: p = 7.3 × 10⁻¹².

Key line: Zero held-out attacks got through, and the attacks that worked were real LLMail emails.

## 8. Does it carry over? A second model and AgentDojo

Does this carry over? (pause) First, a second model family: Qwen2.5-7B on the same held-out set, one run. With no defense 29.3% of attacks worked; with a defense, at most 0.0%. (pause) Second, AgentDojo's workspace suite, a different benchmark with its own tools and attack. One caveat: AgentDojo has no per-task policies, so D2's policy comes from the task's ground truth. That makes D2 an upper bound there.

Key line: Same pattern on a second model and a second benchmark.

## 9. The cost we almost missed: harmless links

Our first benchmark had no normal task with a link in it, so it could not show this cost. (pause) D1h blocks any link copied from an email into a new message, because it cannot tell a colleague's Zoom link from a phishing link. Asking for the link and forwarding the email still always work. (pause) We tried an exploratory fix, D1h-L, after the freeze: a link may go out if the user asks for a link, names the email, and that email came from a contact. It recovers the flow and let no attack through, but a compromised contact account would defeat it. (pause) The reply row fails for a different reason: the model's first move was a reply to an email id that does not exist. Without a defense it got 'no such email' and recovered; with a defense it got a plain refusal and gave up. How a defense refuses matters. Across all 120 link episodes per config.

Key line: Measure the cost on harmless work, not only on attacks.

## 10. Hypotheses scorecard

Scorecard on the held-out set. (pause) The undefended attack rate is 21.8%, below our 30% validity bar; on the LLMail part alone it is 31.7%, because our own attacks never worked. H1, safety: met. H2, usefulness: met, a change of +2.4 points. (pause) Against Dual-LLM: both stopped the same number of attacks, so we cannot call ours safer; the difference is usefulness: D1h+D2 completes significantly more normal tasks.

Key line: H1 met, H2 met, on attacks we never saw.

## 11. What this does not show

Rui again. What our results do not show. (pause) Every attack we ran is fixed: none adapts to our rules, and an attacker who knows them has targets, for example copying an email subject the user is likely to name. Supply-chain attacks, a malicious user, memory that persists across sessions and paraphrased leaks are outside both benchmarks. (pause) These are the next things to test.

Key line: Strong on fixed attacks; adaptive attackers are the open question.

## 12. Takeaways

Three takeaways. (pause) One: decide outside the model. Checking each action in code stopped every attack we ran, with no extra model calls. Two: the two checks do different jobs. D2 removes what the task doesn't need; D1h catches attacker content riding inside an action the user asked for. Three: measure harmless work too. Our first benchmark could not see that D1h blocks copied links. Thank you.

Key line: Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.
